newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo banks ask central bank to lower discount rate.
newsitem.headline: Yugo banks ask central bank to lower discount rate.

text.p: Yugoslav commercial banks are appealing to the central bank to lower its discount rate to enable more lending activity and reduce borrowing costs for companies, Belgrade media reported on Friday.
The appeal came after the Serbian government advised banks to cut operating costs and collect overdue payments in a bid to revive business activity in the troubled economy.
The call from Serbian authorities cleared the way for commercial banks to request the lower discount rate, analysts said.
"We feel this is the most correct stand the government has taken for some time now," Mileta Babovic, Secretary General for the Yugoslav Banking Association (YBA), told Reuters.
The Monetary System Committee of the YBA proposed to the central bank to reduce its discount rate from the current 4.5 percent per month and adjust it to monthly inflation.

Babovic said the relatively stable business environment, with monthly inflation now hovering below 2 percent, gave some space to the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) to cut the discount rate -- which still needed to remain positive in real terms.
With cheaper capital, banks would be able to charge less for their money and increase their credit activity, he said.
"This means more money and cheaper funds to companies short of cash," Babovic added.
The interest rate on banks' borrowing is based on the discount rate increased by a variable percentage.
The central bank controls money supply by the discount rate and, since September, by the (10 percent) reserve requirement.
But Babovic said that the NBY could retain its firm grip over money supply even if the discount rate was lower.
The central bank reduced its key rate to the current level -- corresponding to 68.15 percent a year -- in order to push commercial lending rates down. But those efforts failed.
Babovic said commercial bank lending rates ranged from 10-12 percent per month. The banks set lending rates based on the inflation rate plus 4-5 percent, he said.
Yet rates on the unofficial giro money market -- where banks trade their surplus liquidity -- sometimes go as high as 18 percent per month.
If the spread between borrowing and lending rates was not as high, commercial lending rates would be lower, Babovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
